name: Preferences
plain_language_definition: A rule that lets you write down which outcomes you like more than others — a scoreboard for how much you value each possible result.
everyday_problem: Before anyone starts thinking strategically, we need a way to ask: which outcome does this person actually want? The catch is that outcomes are tangled up. One choice gives you more money but more risk. Another gives you less money but more free time. Before you can ask whether someone makes sense or does best for themselves, you need a way to say how they rank all these mixed-up options.
first_principles_reason: This exists because comparing outcomes requires a base rule. If you cannot rank outcomes, then the words better, worse, or makes sense have nowhere to land. You cannot say someone is trying to do best for themselves without knowing what they count as doing better.
mathematical_principle: A preference is a comparison rule over outcomes. You list each outcome and mark which ones rank above others. A utility function u(x) is a shortcut: instead of writing out all the rankings, you assign each outcome a number, and higher numbers mean ranks you like more. If outcome x gets a higher number than y, that means you prefer x to y — the numbers are just a way to write down the ranking.
why_it_matters: Preferences matter because they are the first simplification the course makes. A real outcome is messy: it mixes money, time, risk, fairness, and emotions. The model cannot carry all that detail, so it keeps just the ranking — which outcomes you prefer to which others. This ranking is the foundation for everything that comes next: payoffs, best moves, and later ideas about whether an outcome was good for someone.
what_breaks_without_it: Without a clear preference ranking, the numbers in a payoff table have no real meaning. Someone could assign them however they want. There is no way to check whether the payoff numbers actually match what the player is trying to do or whether later calculations about their best move are trustworthy.
naive_problem: A naive guess says: people just pick what they like. But the course needs more precision. Your likings have to be steady enough that the model can rely on them across different problems without having to ask you again what better means.
failed_simple_approach: The simple approach breaks down when your rankings loop back on themselves or when small changes in how you describe the choice flip your answer. For instance: you prefer coffee to tea, tea to water, but water to coffee. If that cycle is true, then no stable ranking exists. The model cannot build a consistent best-move rule when someone's preferences go in circles.
mathematical_object: The object is a preference relation: a rule that compares any two outcomes and says which one ranks higher (or if they tie). For this rule to be useful in a model, two things have to be true. First, completeness: you must be able to compare any two outcomes in the problem — no cases where you say I do not know. Second, transitivity: if you rank A above B and B above C, then you must rank A above C — no loops.
operation: List all the outcomes the player might face. Ask them which ones they rank above which others. Collect those rankings. Then test: if you take any three outcomes, do the rankings avoid loops? Can you compare every pair? If yes, the preference is a clean comparison rule and can be represented by numbers.
worked_mini_example: Suppose you rank coffee above tea and tea above water. Transitivity says you must rank coffee above water. That makes sense — if A is better than B and B is better than C, then A is better than C. Without that rule, someone could be tricked into trading around a loop: I trade your coffee for my tea, your tea for my water, your water for my coffee, and now you have less than you started with, even though you were only accepting trades you liked at each step.
lecture_emphasis: This lecture is building a foundation. It is not yet solving games or predicting what people do. It is making sure that when the course later assigns payoff numbers to outcomes, those numbers actually represent a real choice ranking — not just arbitrary scoreboard entries.
common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to think preferences are emotions or moods. In the course, a preference is a disciplined comparison rule: I prefer X to Y means you rank X higher than Y in this model, full stop. It is not a complete picture of your feelings or your life — just the ordering that matters for the problem at hand.
cross_course_connections: This preference ranking is the quiet engine that runs through the whole course. Later, utility functions use it to assign numbers. Payoff tables inherit it to show what each player is trying to get. Bargaining, auction bidding, and choices under uncertainty all depend on having a stable preference ranking as their base layer.
recognize_in_new_work: Look for the place where an economic or strategic model has to say what an actor counts as better or worse before any reasoning about their moves begins.
lecture_depth_walkthrough: The full lecture starts with a simple pressure: before any game starts, people have to choose among outcomes. That means the model needs a way to ask: is outcome A ranked above, below, or tied with outcome B? Completeness means you can compare all the relevant outcomes. Transitivity means the comparisons do not form loops. These are not moral truths about how people should feel. They are the smallest set of rules needed to turn raw likings into a ranking that can be used later in payoff calculations and strategic reasoning.
mathematical_intuition: The math is a shortcut for choice behavior. Instead of memorizing the full story of every outcome, the preference relation keeps just the ordering. A utility function takes that ordering and assigns numbers: higher numbers for outcomes ranked higher. The numbers are a tool — the point is that they preserve the ranking in a form the model can use.
student_trap: Students often get stuck by asking: is this preference realistic for a real human in a real situation? The course is not trying to explain human psychology. It is asking a modeling question: in this problem, can we treat the player's choices as coming from a stable ranking? If yes, we can use that ranking to predict what they will do.
why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because natural language can hide contradictions. You can say you like many things, but a model needs to know whether those likings fit together into one consistent ranking. A preference relation is the smallest formal rule that lets the course check whether your choices are complete and consistent enough to build strategic analysis on top of.
course_boundary_note: Preferences describe what ranks higher within the problem the course is studying. They do not explain why you have those preferences — where your desires come from, or how you learned to like what you like, or whether your preferences might change. If the question is about persuasion, learning, or changing tastes, preference is only the starting point, not the full story.

name: Utility
plain_language_definition: A number attached to each outcome that records how much someone wants it.
everyday_problem: When several people each chase what is best for them, you need to know whether one person will prefer outcome A or outcome B. But you cannot write down a math formula using the words 'I like this more' — math works with numbers. So you have to turn 'A is better than B' into numbers you can actually use in a calculation.
first_principles_reason: Utility exists because strategy and choice need calculation, and calculation needs numbers. If you can write down a single number for each outcome, then you can use arithmetic to find the best move, compare payoffs, or predict what rational people will do.
mathematical_principle: A preference is a ranking — 'I like pizza more than salad.' A utility function is a way to turn that ranking into numbers so math can handle it. If u is a utility function, then u(pizza) = 10 and u(salad) = 5 means 'pizza ranks higher.' The only rule is: a higher number must mean a higher ranking. The actual numbers are up to you — you could use 100 and 20 instead, and it works the same way for ordinary choice.
why_it_matters: Once you turn a ranking into a number, you can put it in a table, calculate averages, compare payoffs, or find the best move when facing risk. Without numbers, the course could only describe outcomes in words. With numbers, the course can actually solve for what rational players do.
what_breaks_without_it: Without numbers, you cannot write a payoff table, calculate expected payoffs when outcomes are uncertain, or find best responses in a game. The course would be stuck describing outcomes without predicting behavior.
naive_problem: The naive reading is that utility is like a fuel gauge inside your brain — higher utility means more happiness, like a real physical thing you can measure. The real reading is that utility is just a label you choose to preserve your ranking, so math can work with it. The number does not have to mean anything except 'this is higher in your preference order.'
failed_simple_approach: It fails when you treat the utility numbers as if they were universal and absolute — like claiming one person's utility of 50 is 'twice as good' as another person's 25. You cannot compare utility numbers across different people, and you cannot change the numbers arbitrarily once you start dealing with risk. A utility function is built for a specific question, and it only works if you use it consistently.
mathematical_object: A utility function u is a machine that takes an outcome (like 'get pizza') and outputs a number. That number is higher when the outcome ranks higher in someone's preference list. The job of u is to preserve the order — nothing more, nothing less.
operation: Pick any numbers that match your ranking, plug them into payoff tables or equations, and use arithmetic to find the best move or the expected outcome.
worked_mini_example: Suppose you rank: pizza first, salad second, soup third. You could assign utilities 10, 5, 0 (gap of 5). Or 100, 20, −7 (uneven gaps). For ordinary choice, both work the same — each ranks outcomes in the same order. But if you face a 50-50 bet between pizza and soup, the numbers matter: with 10 and 0 you get expected utility 5, but with 100 and −7 you get expected utility 46.5. So once risk enters, the gaps between your numbers carry meaning.
lecture_emphasis: The lecture stresses that utility is useful and limited. It turns a vague ranking ('I prefer A') into something a calculator can handle. But it also stresses that utility is just a model choice — the numbers only mean what you design them to mean for that model.
common_misunderstanding: Students often think utility is like height or weight — a real quantity you measure with a ruler. The truth is that utility is whatever numbers you assign to preserve order. An outcome with utility 100 is not 'really' twice as good as one with 50; it just ranks higher. If you never involve risk or comparison across people, the scale is arbitrary.
cross_course_connections: Utility becomes the entry in a payoff table, the value at the end of a decision tree, the expected value in a lottery where outcomes are risky, or the private benefit in an auction. It is the glue between what someone wants and the math that predicts what someone will do.
recognize_in_new_work: Watch for any time a paper or problem turns a goal, payoff, preference, or outcome into a number that can be compared, added up, or optimized. That is utility at work.
lecture_depth_walkthrough: The full picture is this: the course starts with preferences (qualitative — 'I like A better'). Then it needs to do math, so it assigns numbers to outcomes (quantitative — 'A gets a 7, B gets a 3'). That mapping from outcomes to numbers is utility. Once numbers are in place, the course can use algebra: set up payoff tables, calculate expected values, find best responses by maximizing. The key constraint is that utility is a representation chosen for the job at hand. It is not a universal truth. Different problems might assign different utilities to the same outcome. When only choice matters (no risk), the numbers are arbitrary — you only need the ranking. When risk enters (lotteries, betting, insurance), the gaps between numbers start to matter, and the utility function has to preserve more structure so that averaging (expected value) works the way you want.
mathematical_intuition: Utility is the machine that lets you swap a ranking into a number, so arithmetic can take over from words. Once you have numbers, you can ask: which move gives the highest expected payoff? The danger is forgetting what utility does and does not do — it preserves order and (under risk) preserves the right averages, but it does not tell you which utilities are 'real' or comparable across people.
student_trap: Students often think utility is money or happiness — something real that you can add up. Then they get confused when a utility of 100 does not mean 'twice as happy' as 50, or when one person's utility of 50 has nothing to do with another person's. The cure is to remember: utility is a number you pick to represent a ranking and make it computable.
why_math_has_to_exist: Tables, graphs, and equations need numbers to work. You cannot plug words into a formula. Utility is the translator from 'I want this' to a number, so the course can calculate what rational behavior looks like. It is the handle that moves from 'prefer' to 'has the larger payoff.'
course_boundary_note: Utility is a tool for one game or one problem at a time. It preserves your ranking and (when risk is involved) your preferences over bets. It does not automatically transfer to other people's preferences, and changing the numbers arbitrarily can break the model if risk is part of the question.

name: Expected Utility
plain_language_definition: When you face an uncertain choice, expected utility is the score you calculate by adding up (outcome score × its probability) for every possible result.
everyday_problem: You often must decide before you know what will happen: will a bid win or lose? Will a risky investment pay off or lose money? Will someone turn out to be honest or dishonest? You need a way to compare choices when the future is uncertain.
first_principles_reason: This exists because people choose now but outcomes arrive later. You cannot wait to see which result happens before deciding—you have to pick an action today. So your choice has to measure the whole range of possible futures, not just the one that happens to occur.
mathematical_principle: Your belief about the unknown is shown as a probability distribution—a list of possible states or types with a number (the probability) for each. The calculation is E[u(a, θ)] = Σ_θ p(θ) u(a, θ). In plain terms: θ is the unknown state or type; p(θ) is how likely you think it is; multiply each payoff by its probability and add them all up.
why_it_matters: In strategic games, choices often happen before uncertainty clears. You compare actions that might lead to many different payoffs depending on what others do or what hidden information turns out to be true. Expected utility gives you one number to compare all those options.
what_breaks_without_it: Without expected utility, games where players have hidden information—like auctions or contract negotiations—would have no clear way to score an action. You could not reason about what a rational player would do when they do not know the full picture.
naive_problem: A naive choice picks whichever outcome sounds best and ignores how likely it is. The right way is to ask: how much should each possible outcome count in my decision, given that I am not sure which one will happen?
failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when a tempting payoff is nearly impossible or a modest payoff is almost certain. A one-in-a-million jackpot should not beat a guaranteed small win. Probability must change the choice—the decision is over a gamble, not a known result.
mathematical_object: Expected utility is the number you get when you weight each possible payoff by its probability and sum them. It squeezes a risky situation down to one score so you can compare choices.
operation: List each possible outcome. Write the payoff (utility) for that outcome. Write the probability you assign to it. Multiply payoff times probability for each outcome. Add all the products together.
worked_mini_example: A bidder expects to win 1 out of 3 times with a payoff of 90, and lose 2 out of 3 times with a payoff of 0. The expected utility is (1/3)(90) + (2/3)(0) = 30. This tells the bidder whether placing that bid is better than other bids under the whole distribution of possible wins and losses.
lecture_emphasis: The lecture shows how expected utility lets you reason about uncertainty without pretending it goes away. Probabilities and payoff numbers appear together in one formula so that probability shapes the choice the way it should.
common_misunderstanding: A trap is to average dollar amounts directly. But if you care about risk—if, say, having money is worth less to you when you already have a lot—then the payoff (utility) per dollar is not the same across amounts. You must use payoff, not dollars, in the average.
cross_course_connections: Expected utility is the foundation under mixed strategies, Bayesian Nash equilibrium, auctions, and belief updates. Anywhere in the course a type or action is unknown, or where a player acts before information arrives, this is the tool underneath.
recognize_in_new_work: Look for private information, uncertain types, lotteries, or risk where the model must add up payoffs across multiple possible worlds weighted by beliefs.
lecture_depth_walkthrough: In deeper work, expected utility unlocks private-information games. When you do not know a rival's cost, valuation, or signal, you assign a probability to each possibility—a belief—and average your payoffs across that belief. This is how auctions work: a bidder does not know what others will bid, so she computes expected utility by taking each possible rival bid, weighing it by the probability she assigns to it, and summing the payoff times probability for each. The same logic applies to mechanism design: a mechanism builder must pay players enough to compensate them for the risk of hidden information about others. At this level, expected utility is not just an average—it is the language that ties together beliefs, incentives, and choice under uncertainty into one coherent model.
mathematical_intuition: Think of expected utility as a weighted ledger. Each possible payoff contributes to your total in proportion to how likely you think that state is. The expectation symbol E[·] is not mysterious—it just means: write down each possible world, multiply its payoff by its probability, and add all those products up.
student_trap: Two common traps: students sometimes average dollar amounts when they should average payoff (utility) amounts, because payoff measures what you care about, not the raw dollars. Also, students forget that probabilities come from your belief before you know the answer—they are not frequencies from looking back at what already happened.
why_math_has_to_exist: Uncertainty creates a bundle of possible outcomes. You choose now and find out later which one happens. You cannot optimize separately for each future state—you need one score for the whole risky action. Expected utility is that one score, built by summing (payoff × probability) over all possibilities you assign a belief to.
course_boundary_note: The boundary of expected utility is its own limits: it is a disciplined way to average payoffs, but it does not check whether your beliefs are correct or whether you are right to be risk-neutral. If your probabilities are wrong or your utility function does not match how you actually feel about risk, expected utility will optimize you toward the wrong goal.

name: Strategic Form Games
plain_language_definition: A table where you write down all the players, all the moves each one can make, and the score each player gets from every possible combination of moves.
everyday_problem: Imagine you and your friend each need to choose something at the exact same moment, without knowing what the other chose. But once you both decide, what you get depends on both choices together. How do you show what's really going on? You need a table that captures the fact that nobody gets to see the other's choice before picking their own.
first_principles_reason: Strategic dependence means your payoff hangs on everyone's move at once, not just your own. A story told in words hides what each player can control and what result each combination of moves creates. A clear record — who chooses what, and what each combination delivers — is the only way to compare what each person should do.
mathematical_principle: A payoff function u_i(a_i, a_-i) assigns a score to player i. Here is what each symbol means: i is one player; a_i is that player's action; a_-i means all the other players' actions taken together; u_i is the number (payoff) that player i receives. The full action profile is (a_i, a_-i) — everyone's action at once — and that determines what score player i walks away with.
why_it_matters: By putting all players, all available moves, and all payoffs into one table, the course can ask sharp questions: Does one move beat another no matter what others do? If you think others will choose a certain way, what move gives you the highest score? Can everyone settle on choices where nobody wants to switch? The table holds all these questions at once without losing track of who affects whom.
what_breaks_without_it: If you only describe a game in words — a story about two people who want different things — you can talk about what seems good in theory, but you lack the structure to check your claim. You cannot easily compare what happens when player 1 chooses A versus B, or see which payoff pairs are possible. A table lets you check these things row by row and cell by cell.
naive_problem: Naively, you might just tell a story: two people each want something different, and the outcome depends on how they guess about each other. But that's vague. The course needs precision: a concrete list of every move available to each player, and a concrete number showing what each player gets at every possible move pair.
failed_simple_approach: If you only describe moves without a table, a move can sound good in one paragraph but actually give a different payoff under different circumstances. A table forces you to see every move inside every context — paired with every move the opponent might make.
mathematical_object: The thing you build is called a normal-form game. It collects: a list of all players, the set of moves each player can pick, and a payoff function that assigns a score to each player for every possible profile (i.e., every combination of moves, one from each player).
operation: To build a strategic form game: (1) name all the players; (2) list which moves are available to each player; (3) fill in a payoff number for each player at every cell, where a cell is one complete move profile — one combination of moves, one move per player.
worked_mini_example: Prisoner's dilemma: two players, each chooses confess or stay silent. One cell shows both chose confess; another shows both stayed silent; another shows player 1 confessed while player 2 stayed silent. Each cell holds two payoffs, one for each player. The payoff inside a cell comes from the pair of moves, not from one move in isolation.
lecture_emphasis: This is the first serious tool the course uses to write down an interactive situation. The table is not a pretty decoration; it is the actual working machine. Rows are all the moves player 1 can make; columns are all the moves player 2 can make. Each cell is what each player receives when that move pair happens. Once the table exists, you can ask dominance, best-response, and Nash questions by looking at rows, columns, and cells.
common_misunderstanding: A common trap is to look at one row of the table and think the other player does not matter. That is wrong. Each row has multiple cells because the other player has multiple choices. You cannot say a move is good until you specify: good against which opponent move? The whole point of the table is to show that every payoff comes from both players choosing at once.
cross_course_connections: Strategic form is the foundation. Dominance (one move beats another for you no matter what they do), best response (the move that gives you the highest score against their expected choice), Nash equilibrium (a move pair where neither player wants to switch), and mixed strategies (flipping a coin on purpose to stay unpredictable) can all be checked by reading the table. When timing matters or you have information your opponent lacks, later chapters use trees and Bayesian games, which are extensions of this table representation.
recognize_in_new_work: When you see a problem where two or more agents choose at the same time (or nearly so), where each agent's payoff depends on everyone's choice, and where the exact order of moves or who knows what information is not the main point, you are looking at a situation that fits strategic form. Look for payoff matrices, simultaneous moves, or models where timing is compressed so that strategic dependence — the fact that my payoff hangs on your choice — becomes the main thing to understand.
lecture_depth_walkthrough: The deep version builds this slowly. A strategic-form game lists all players, all actions each can take, and a payoff number for each player at each action profile. This works because it forces you to write down the interaction: my move and your move together. Once written down in a table, the interaction becomes visible and checkable. You can ask: is my move a best response to your likely move? Is there a move pair where nobody wants to switch? Can I survive by mixing my choices randomly? The table is not optional when every payoff depends on everyone's action at once.
mathematical_intuition: Think of a payoff function as a machine: you feed it everyone's action (the full profile), and it spits out a score for each player. The input is not a single choice; it is a complete picture of what each player does. The output can be different for each player — the same cell might look wonderful to player 1 but terrible to player 2. That is why you cannot evaluate a move in a vacuum; you need to see it inside the table.
student_trap: Students often think a row of the table has one value and one meaning. That is wrong. A row shows what happens to player 1 across all of player 2's possible moves. Player 1's payoff in that row changes depending on which column you are in — which move player 2 picked. So a move cannot be judged as good or bad until you ask: good or bad against which opponent move? The table has multiple values per row because the opponent has choices.
why_math_has_to_exist: You cannot avoid this representation. Once every payoff depends on every player's action at once — on the full profile — you need a thing that holds all those dependencies in one place and makes them visible. Words scatter the information across a story. A table collects it so you can ask a clear question: if player 1 changes their move from A to B while player 2 stays the same, does player 1 do better or worse? The table lets you check this without confusion.
course_boundary_note: The edge of what strategic form can show clearly is timing and hidden information. If one player moves before another and can see their choice, or if a player has private information that changes their payoffs, the table hides those wrinkles unless you carefully write them into your definition of what a move is. Later representations like game trees and Bayesian games handle those explicitly.

name: Extensive Form Games
plain_language_definition: A game drawn as a tree diagram instead of a table, because the timing of moves and what each player knows at each moment matter.
everyday_problem: In real conflicts, people move one at a time, not all at once. A choice made later can depend on what happened earlier. And sometimes you know more than the other person — or they know more than you. A flat table misses all of that.
first_principles_reason: Time and information are real. If you move first, you cannot take back your choice. If you move second, you might have seen what the first person did. These facts change whether a threat is believable or a promise is honest.
mathematical_principle: Backward induction starts at the end. At the final decision point, a player chooses the branch that gives the best score. Then move back one step: knowing what the later player will do, what should the earlier player choose? Keep going backward to the start. The formula is `V(node) = max_action V(next node)`, which means: the value of where you stand is the highest value you can reach by picking one of your moves.
why_it_matters: A tree lets you see credibility. If you threaten to do something costly if the other person acts, the tree shows whether you would actually do it when that moment arrives. It also shows what each player observes: did you see the other person's move, or did you move blind? That shape of information changes everything.
what_breaks_without_it: Without a tree, you would write down all actions in rows and columns, like a table. But that table pretends everyone moved at the same time and saw nothing. It would hide whether a threat is really believable, whether later moves were made with information about earlier ones, and whether a player could distinguish between different situations.
naive_problem: A naive list just says what each person can do, with no order. It ignores when moves happen and what is known at each step. If you want to know whether a threat will work, you have to ask: will the person carrying out the threat actually want to do it when the time comes?
failed_simple_approach: A simple payoff table treats everything as if it happens at once, no history, no secrets. In reality, a threat made at the start may look good on paper. But when the threatened moment actually arrives, the person who makes the threat might no longer want to follow through because the cost is too real. The tree forces you to check that.
mathematical_object: The object is a tree: starting point, branches for each choice, nodes where decisions happen, a record of what happened so far, sets of nodes that a player cannot tell apart (because they do not know which one they are in), and numbers at the endpoints showing each player's score.
operation: Draw branches for the order of moves. At each node, note what the player at that node knows — can they see what happened before, or do they move blind to earlier choices? Then reason backward from the end: each player picks the move that gives the highest score when that node is reached, assuming future moves will also be smart. Or reason forward using beliefs: if a player cannot see the history, what would they believe happened?
worked_mini_example: A new firm thinks about entering a market. The incumbent (the company already there) says, 'If you enter, I will cut prices and hurt us both.' The tree shows two paths: the new firm enters, then the incumbent chooses between a price war and peaceful coexistence. The tree asks: if entry happened, would the incumbent really cut prices, or does the threat fall apart because a price war now costs the incumbent too much?
lecture_emphasis: The tree is a teaching tool. Nodes show decision points. Branches show choices. Information sets show what a player knows or cannot tell apart. Together, they make it visible who moves when, what is observed, and where credibility gets tested.
common_misunderstanding: A common mistake is to collapse the tree into a simple table and lose the question of credibility. If the tree showed a threat made at the start, the table might treat it as binding forever. But the tree reveals that threats can become non-credible as the game unfolds.
cross_course_connections: Extensive form connects to backward induction (reasoning from end to start), subgame perfection (each subgame must be solved correctly), bargaining with time (offers and counteroffers), one-shot deviation (checking whether a player can gain by changing only one move), and PBE (perfect Bayesian equilibrium, which updates beliefs as the tree unfolds). All of these need a tree to make sense.
recognize_in_new_work: Look for any situation where the order of moves changes what a person would do, or where a player does not have full information about what happened before. Look for threats or promises that depend on what happens later. Look for a claim about strategy or a prediction that assumes simultaneous moves when the actual sequence was different.
lecture_depth_walkthrough: The deep version asks what a table cannot show. If players move in sequence, the tree marks it. If a player observes an earlier choice, the tree marks it—different branches lead to nodes that the player can tell apart. If a player moves blind (does not know what happened), the tree groups nodes into an information set so the player must choose the same move at both nodes. Terminal nodes show payoffs. This is not just a picture. It is the structure that lets you ask whether a threat is believable (will it be chosen later?) and whether beliefs must shift (what would a player infer from an unexpected move?).
mathematical_intuition: The key idea is nesting: one game sits inside another. A node represents a history (the path taken so far). An action picks a branch. A terminal path gives scores. This structure lets you reason recursively — solve the end first, then work backward, knowing that each earlier player predicts the smart moves of later players.
student_trap: Students often assume that a tree automatically means every player saw every earlier move. That is wrong. Information sets are the remedy. An information set groups nodes together because a player at those nodes cannot tell them apart — they might be at node A or node B, but they do not know which. So they must choose the same move at both.
why_math_has_to_exist: A flat list of actions cannot encode time or information. It cannot say who moved first, what was observed, or which histories look identical to a player. The tree structure preserves those facts as explicit objects—nodes, edges, information sets, payoffs—so that later reasoning about credibility and belief updates has a home.
course_boundary_note: The boundary is honesty about information and sequence. A tree works only if its nodes, information sets, and payoffs truly reflect what each player can observe and choose at each point in time.

name: Dominance
plain_language_definition: A test to cross off moves that are worse than some other move in every possible situation your opponent faces you with.
everyday_problem: In any game, some moves are just worse. They lose to another move no matter what the other person tries. But if you list all possible moves, the bad ones can hide the real choices that matter. Dominance lets you cross off the hopeless ones first.
first_principles_reason: You can sometimes reject a move without guessing what the other side will do. If one move always beats another move — no matter which choice the opponent makes — then the losing move is dead weight. You do not need to predict the opponent to trash it.
mathematical_principle: The math compares two moves by looking at what each one gives you against every possible opponent move. Write it as: move A dominates move B if your score from A is always at least as high as your score from B, and sometimes strictly higher. The inequality holds for every opponent choice; that is what makes it dominance.
why_it_matters: This is one of the few places where clear thinking alone — without any belief about the opponent — tells you a move is bad. If you can prove a move loses in every case, you can eliminate it before you even think about best responses or equilibrium. This makes the problem smaller and cleaner.
what_breaks_without_it: If you keep every possible move alive, the board stays cluttered. Some moves have no reason to exist, but they still sit in the analysis like noise. Without dominance, you would not know which moves to ignore first, so finding the real strategic solution gets harder before you ever reach concepts like best response.
naive_problem: A wrong way is to cross off a move because it sounds bad or you think the opponent is unlikely to set you up in a certain way. Dominance is stricter than a guess. It says: prove that this move loses to another move in literally every single scenario the opponent can put you in.
failed_simple_approach: The simple approach breaks when a move is awful against one opponent choice but actually good against another. That is not dominance — that is a tradeoff that depends on your belief about what the opponent will do. Those cases need a more advanced tool, like best response or rationalizability.
mathematical_object: The object is a pair of two moves, where one move wins against the other no matter what the opponent does. More formally: you can represent it as a relation, a set of ordered pairs (A, B) where move A dominates move B. To check if it works, look at your payoff table row by row (or column by column if you are the one being compared). If every number in row A is at least as large as the corresponding number in row B, and at least one number is strictly larger, then A dominates B. You can mark these pairs on the game matrix to see at a glance which moves are dead.
operation: Pick two moves and line them up. Compare the score you get from each one against every single opponent action. If the first move never gives you less than the second move, and at least once gives you strictly more, then the first move dominates the second.
worked_mini_example: Suppose you are a shop owner and can price high or low. If pricing low always makes you more money than pricing high — whether your rival prices low or high — then high pricing is dominated. You cross it off without having to guess what the rival will do.
lecture_emphasis: The dominance lecture teaches you to cross off moves by math, not by intuition. The rule is: check every possible opponent move before you say a move is not worth playing. If you skip even one opponent scenario, you have not proven dominance.
common_misunderstanding: People often think a move is dominated because it seems unlikely to work or because they do not like it. Real dominance means you compare across all opponent moves and prove it is always worse. A move that is bad under one opponent choice but useful under another is not dominated — that is a belief problem, not a dominance problem.
cross_course_connections: Dominance is the start of a chain. After dominance, you move to iterated deletion (cross off dominated moves, then check again) and rationalizability (what moves could a thinking opponent play). Both use dominance as a building block. Dominance also explains why dominated strategies do not appear in equilibrium — no rational player would ever pick a move that is dominated.
recognize_in_new_work: When you see an argument that crosses off a move before computing equilibrium — because one move always loses to another — you are seeing dominance at work.
lecture_depth_walkthrough: The full lecture shows a rare moment: you can throw out a move without any belief about the opponent. To test dominance, take two moves and compare them against every possible opponent response. If one move always scores at least as high as the other, and sometimes strictly higher, the inferior move is gone. The key phrase is 'against every possible opponent response' — that universal check is what makes dominance so strong but also so rare. Most moves are not dominated even though they might fail other tests later on.
mathematical_intuition: The intuition behind the math is a single comparison that works everywhere. You line up two moves and check the payoff in each column (or row). If one move's payoff is always bigger or equal, dominance holds. Because the comparison does not change from one opponent choice to another, no belief can save the dominated move.
student_trap: A common trap is deleting a move because it performs badly when you guess the opponent will do something specific. That is not dominance. If the move is bad only against one opponent choice but good against others, it is not dominated — you just dislike it under your own prediction of what the opponent will do.
why_math_has_to_exist: Math exists here because some moves can be thrown out by proof, not by guess. Dominance formalizes 'no matter what the opponent does' as a list of inequalities. Each inequality is a check against one opponent move. If all the inequalities pass, you have a mathematical fact that the move is dominated, and no amount of belief-changing will fix it.
course_boundary_note: Dominance is powerful when it applies, but it does not cover everything. Many moves are alive because they are not dominated — even though they might fail a best response test or not appear in equilibrium. That is where other tools take over: beliefs about the opponent, best responses to those beliefs, and finally equilibrium where beliefs and moves reinforce each other.

name: Iterated Deletion
plain_language_definition: A process where you remove strategies that are clearly bad, then look at the smaller game left behind and remove new strategies that are now bad in this smaller game, and keep repeating until nothing more can be removed.
everyday_problem: When you remove one bad move, the game changes—what was once a decent move might now be a bad move in the smaller game. This keeps happening in waves: you delete, the game shrinks, new bad moves appear, you delete again.
first_principles_reason: This exists because when people think strategically, they think recursively. You can reason: I won't pick this move because it's bad. Then I know they won't pick it, so I can ignore it. But now my own choices look different because some of their options are gone. Then they can reason that you see this, and your choices look different to them. Reasoning about each other's reasoning creates layers.
mathematical_principle: Dominance is comparing two strategies by checking whether one is always at least as good as the other across all the moves the other players might make. The technical check is: strategy s dominates strategy t if the score from s is always greater than or equal to the score from t, no matter what the other players choose, and sometimes strictly greater. In plain terms: one strategy beats another in every single scenario the other players create.
why_it_matters: Strategic reasoning has layers when people think about what others will do. Removing one unreasonable choice can make another choice unreasonable in the resulting smaller game, so understanding what's reasonable can spread through the whole table like a chain reaction. This is how you narrow down from many possible strategies to a few plausible ones.
what_breaks_without_it: Without iterated deletion, you miss how reasoning about one round changes what's reasonable in the next round. Some games look very complicated until you remove the obviously bad moves—then the pattern of what makes sense becomes clearer. You'd be stuck looking at all possible choices at once instead of understanding how rationality can narrow them down step by step.
naive_problem: A naive approach removes the bad moves once and stops, treating the smaller game as just an accounting exercise. The real reasoning asks: after we remove those bad moves, what do the remaining players now understand? Does that new understanding make any of the remaining moves unreasonable? This recursive question is where the procedure gets its power.
failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when students treat the deletion as just crossing off a row or column in a table, instead of reasoning about what players can infer from the fact that everyone is being rational. Each deletion round means all the players understand that earlier obviously-bad moves have been ruled out, so the expectations about what others will do have changed.
mathematical_object: The mathematical object is a game that gets smaller with each step—you start with all possible strategies, remove the dominated ones, and create a reduced game with only the surviving strategies, then repeat the dominance check on this reduced version.
operation: Apply the dominance rule to find strategies that are always worse than some other strategy. Delete those strategies. Build a new, smaller game from what's left. Check the dominance rule again on the smaller game. Keep repeating this process until no more dominated strategies exist under the dominance rule you're using.
worked_mini_example: Imagine a guessing game where players guess numbers from 0 to 100. A guess of 100 is unreasonable because no rational person would guess that. Remove all guesses of 100. Now 99 looks unreasonable for the same reason—no one will guess 100, so no one can justify guessing 99. Remove it. Keep removing guesses from the top downward. The process spirals inward, showing why only very low guesses survive rational reasoning.
lecture_emphasis: The lecture uses this process to show that assumptions about rationality can build on each other. The operation itself is straightforward—cross off bad strategies, rebuild, repeat—but the meaning is deeper: it shows how one person's rationality can force another person's hand, which then forces the first person's hand again, and so on.
common_misunderstanding: A big mistake is ignoring the difference between strict dominance and weak dominance. Strict dominance means one strategy is strictly better in every scenario. Weak dominance means one strategy is better-or-equal in every scenario and strictly better in at least one. With weak dominance, the order in which you delete strategies can change what survives, so you have to be careful about which version you're using.
cross_course_connections: Iterated deletion connects to dominance (the idea of one move being worse than another) and to rationalizability (what beliefs about others' moves allow you to justify a move). It also shows what common knowledge means: if everyone knows everyone is rational, and everyone knows everyone knows this, the deletion process can go many rounds. But iterated deletion is different from Nash equilibrium—deletion can narrow down the game before you find an equilibrium, but it doesn't always point to one unique answer for what will happen.
recognize_in_new_work: Look for elimination arguments that remove options in stages, where each stage uses the assumption that others are rational. When you see 'a player would not do X because that would only make sense if an opponent did Y, but the opponent would not do Y,' you are watching iterated reasoning. Find patterns where an action is ruled out based on what remains after earlier eliminations, not just a one-time comparison.
lecture_depth_walkthrough: The deep version adds reasoning about reasoning. Dominance compares strategies directly, but after you delete some of them, the remaining game is psychologically different—your opponent has fewer real options. A strategy that wasn't dominated in the original game might become dominated in the smaller game because some of your opponent's options disappeared. This creates a chain: I eliminate your bad moves, you understand I did that, so you eliminate my moves that were only reasonable when your bad moves were possible, and so on. The process is mechanical—apply a rule, shrink the game, repeat—but its meaning depends on players understanding rationality and understanding that others understand rationality too.
mathematical_intuition: Think of the game as a shrinking action set. Start with all possible moves for all players. Apply dominance to find and remove bad strategies. Now the game is smaller. Apply dominance again to this reduced version—the comparisons change because fewer opponent options exist. Apply once more. Each round, the domain of what the other players might do gets smaller, so the comparison of whether your strategy is good shifts. This is repeated trimming of a shrinking problem.
student_trap: Students often gloss over whether the game uses strict or weak dominance and whether the order of deletions matters. These are not details—with weak dominance especially, different deletion orders can leave different strategies alive, so the lecture distinction between strict and weak is crucial. Saying 'we deleted' is not enough; you need to know which deletion rule was applied and what remained.
why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object exists because rationality can nest. Once you eliminate one choice as unreasonable, the remaining game changes, and what was reasonable before might become unreasonable now. Iterated deletion is the formal procedure that tracks this shrinking action set carefully and systematically, rather than relying on informal intuition about multiple rounds of thinking. It forces you to be precise about what is eliminated and why, and what that elimination means for the next round.
course_boundary_note: The boundary is which dominance rule you use—strict or weak—because they have different logical force. Strict dominance can never create a different result based on deletion order, but weak dominance can. Common knowledge assumptions also matter: how many rounds of 'everyone knows everyone is rational' can you assume? These boundary choices affect what gets eliminated and what survives. The lecture distinguishes the procedure from equilibrium selection because surviving iterated deletion does not mean a strategy will be played; it only means the strategy has not been ruled out by this particular rationality test.

name: Rationalizability
plain_language_definition: A strategy is defensible if there exists some reasonable belief about the other players that would make this strategy give you the highest possible payoff — the score or outcome you care about. Your move doesn't have to be what experts predict. It just has to be what some rational expectation could justify.
everyday_problem: Deciding which strategies make sense to consider without assuming everyone has reached one locked-in agreement about what will happen. You need a test that catches strategies people might reasonably choose before you check whether all their choices can fit together perfectly.
first_principles_reason: A strategy can be rational for someone who holds one particular belief about others, even when that strategy does not appear in the final prediction of what everyone will do. The course uses this idea because Nash equilibrium is only one possible anchor for what strategies to take seriously. You need a wider net first.
mathematical_principle: A belief is a probability assignment—a guess about how likely each possible situation or type is. The key formula is E[u(a, theta)] = sum_theta p(theta) u(a, theta). In plain words: 'a' is your action; 'theta' is the unknown situation; 'p(theta)' is your guess about how likely that situation is; 'u(a, theta)' is the score you get from action 'a' when situation 'theta' occurs. The expected value adds up: multiply each payoff by its probability, then sum. This tells you the average score you expect.
why_it_matters: Because not every strategy that makes sense under some belief has to show up in Nash equilibrium. You often need to ask: could this move be optimal for someone who holds a different belief than the analyst does? Rationalizability gives you that question.
what_breaks_without_it: Without it, students jump straight from strategies that are never good to Nash equilibrium strategies—skipping the middle ground. They miss that a strategy can survive because one player could hold a coherent belief that makes it their best move, even if that belief turns out not to match everyone else's choices in the final prediction.
naive_problem: A naive view says an unexpected move is irrational just because the person looking at it didn't foresee it. Rationalizability asks a harder question: could there exist any coherent belief that would make this move your best response? The difference matters because rational people can disagree on beliefs.
failed_simple_approach: The simple approach treats the analyst's own forecast as the only reasonable belief to consider. But game theory must separate unreasonable actions from actions that are reasonable if different players expect different things. Two people can both be rational and yet not expect what an outside observer would predict.
mathematical_object: A set—a list—of strategies where each surviving strategy has the property that it can be a best response to some belief about which of the other surviving strategies the other players will use. You build this set step by step: keep only strategies that are best responses to some probability distribution over the remaining strategies.
operation: For each strategy a player might use: ask whether there exists any probability distribution over the other players' surviving strategies such that strategy A gives the highest expected payoff. If yes, the strategy survives. If no such belief makes it optimal, delete it and move to the next round.
worked_mini_example: Your opponent might choose left or right. You are considering action X. Your first instinct is that X is bad because you expect opponent to go right. But the rationalizability question is not about your expectation. It is: could opponent be likely to go left? If opponent goes left and you pick X, do you get a higher payoff than your other options? If yes, then even though you personally would guess right, the belief 'opponent will go left' is coherent enough to make X optimal. So X survives rationalizability. The strategy doesn't have to match your favorite forecast—it just has to be somebody's best response under some defensible belief.
lecture_emphasis: The lecture shifts the focus from striking down impossible moves to explaining which moves can be defended. Instead of asking 'is this what will happen?' the rationalizability lecture asks 'could this be sensible under some belief?' Beliefs are no longer hidden background; they become the explicit reason why a strategy stays alive.
common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to read rationalizable as synonymous with predicted or correct. It means defensible under some belief. Many rationalizable strategies will never occur because players' actual beliefs point elsewhere. Rationalizable is broader and intentionally weaker than the final prediction.
cross_course_connections: Rationalizability keeps the best-response idea from Nash equilibrium but loosens the requirement that everyone must be right about each other's choices. It also foreshadows Bayesian thinking because beliefs—probabilities over types or situations—become the explicit object that justifies choice, not just invisible background intuition.
recognize_in_new_work: Watch for models that separate clearly impossible behavior—strategies that are never best responses to any belief—from behavior that is one of several plausible responses under different expectations. Any analysis that asks whether a strategy could be justified by some coherent belief is invoking rationalizability.
lecture_depth_walkthrough: Rationalizability sits between dominance and Nash equilibrium in the progression. Dominance asks: is there any state of the world where this action is worth taking? If not, delete it. Nash asks: is there one mutually consistent agreement where each player does what is optimal given the actual choices of others? Rationalizability occupies the middle: keep a strategy if it could be optimal under some belief about what the other players will choose. The lecture builds this by first recalling what a belief is—a probability guess. Then it shows that the belief is not decoration. It is the structural reason the strategy survives. But belief is not enough on its own; the strategy still must maximize expected payoff given that belief. Best response is still the test. The strategy has to be someone's optimal choice under that particular belief, not just a move a player might randomly try.
mathematical_intuition: The intuition is that coherence of belief supports the strategy. Rather than checking whether all players' strategies and beliefs agree in one final picture, you ask whether a single strategy can be justified by at least one belief. That belief is a probability distribution over what others do. The strategy is rationalizable if there exists such a distribution where it maximizes expected payoff. Existence—not uniqueness, not everyone else agreeing—is what matters.
student_trap: Students often get stuck because rationalizability feels permissive—like anything goes. It is permissive on purpose: it widens the net before you lock down predictions. But it is not empty. A strategy still has to be a best response to some belief. You cannot just claim a move is rational because someone somewhere might pick it. It has to be optimal under that belief, which means it must yield a higher expected payoff than the alternative moves.
why_math_has_to_exist: Because plausibility depends on belief. A move can look odd from outside and still be rational for someone who expects opponents to behave differently. Normal language tends to lump surprising, wrong, irrational, and off-the-equilibrium-path into one bucket. Rationalizability separates them. The math must exist because the question—does there exist a probability distribution over surviving opponent strategies such that this action maximizes expected payoff—requires checking an infinite space of possible beliefs. Ordinary reasoning cannot track this precisely. The math asks for existence: there must be at least one coherent belief that supports the move. The belief does not have to be the analyst's best guess or shared by everyone. It just has to be coherent enough to make the action optimal.
course_boundary_note: The boundary is mutual consistency. Rationalizability can justify a strategy from a single player's point of view. It does not require all players' beliefs to be true at the same time. A rationalizable strategy may survive because one belief supports it, while the beliefs of the other players conflict with that belief or conflict with each other. Nash equilibrium, by contrast, requires each player's strategy to be a best response to the actual strategies in the proposed outcome, and all beliefs must be correct. That is why rationalizability is useful as a wider criterion but deliberately weaker than equilibrium as a solution concept.

name: Best Response
plain_language_definition: Your best move when you know (or guess) what someone else will do. It is the action that gives you the highest score given their move.
everyday_problem: When you are trying to decide what to do, you cannot just pick any move and say it is 'good.' A move that works beautifully against one person's choice can fail miserably against another. The same action is good or bad depending on what the other person does.
first_principles_reason: Choices in strategic situations are not made in a vacuum. They are made against someone else's action. The same move has different outcomes depending on the opponent, so what is best for you always depends on what you think they will do.
mathematical_principle: The best-response set for player i, written BR_i(a_-i), is the collection of actions that maximize player i's payoff when the other players choose a_-i. In symbols: BR_i(a_-i) = argmax_a u_i(a, a_-i). Here argmax is a command that means: look at all your available actions, calculate your payoff for each one, and pick the action (or actions) with the highest payoff.
why_it_matters: Best response is the foundation of strategic thinking. Before talking about when both players' moves are stable, the course must answer the simpler question: if the world is set up this way (opponent does X), which move gives me the best score? This small conditional calculation appears again and again—hidden inside every equilibrium check, every auction rule, every mixed-strategy computation, and every dynamic negotiation.
what_breaks_without_it: Without best response, there is no way to test whether an equilibrium is real. You could not check whether two strategies are stable against each other, you could not verify auction bids, you could not build mixed strategies, and you could not plan what to do in situations that have already partially unfolded.
naive_problem: A naive question is: is this action rational? That skips the most important part. Rational given what? Rational against which opponent move? Rational with which belief? Rational if the game has or has not already started? The missing condition is where the real strategic thinking happens.
failed_simple_approach: A simple approach fails because the same action is not always right. Cutting your price can be wise if rivals stay high, but disastrous if they cut too. Bidding high can win you a deal, but lose money if everyone bids high. Sending a cheap signal works if rivals believe it, but fails if they think it is a lie. The action that is best depends on what the opponent does.
mathematical_object: The best-response set is a collection: all the actions that maximize a player's payoff when everyone else's actions (or the player's beliefs about those actions) are pinned down. It stores the answer to the question: given that they do this, which of my moves is best?
operation: Take a step: assume the opponent does a specific thing (or has a specific type, or has a specific belief). Now compare every action available to you. For each action, compute your payoff. Select the action or actions with the largest payoff. Those are your best responses to that opponent move or belief.
worked_mini_example: A store is deciding on its price. If it believes its competitor will keep prices high, the store might also keep prices high and share profitable customers. But if the store learns the competitor will slash prices, the store's best move changes—it might cut its own prices to stay competitive. The best response is different each time because the opponent's action changed.
lecture_emphasis: The best-response lecture teaches the repeated micro-operation that will drive the rest of the course. It shows how to take a condition (the opponent's move or a belief about the opponent) and compute the highest-scoring action. This tiny operation is built into reaction curves, equilibrium verification, auction theory, and dynamic play.
common_misunderstanding: Students often say an action is rational without completing the thought. They forget to say: rational against what belief or move? That missing phrase hides the real assumption. The best-response idea forces the student to always name the condition.
cross_course_connections: Best response appears in Nash equilibrium (each player's move must be a best response to the others), in mixed strategies (you randomize to make the opponent indifferent, so no response is strictly better), in auction design (you bid your best response to your belief about others' values), in dynamic games (at each decision point you choose a best response to future play), and in mechanism design (you design payoffs so honest choices are best responses).
recognize_in_new_work: When you read a paper or a new game, look for the step where someone says if player A does this, then player B should do that. Those words signal a best response. Look for reaction functions (curves showing what one player should do in response to another). Look for optimization steps that start with given. Whenever you see given, a best response is hiding inside.
lecture_depth_walkthrough: The deeper story: a best response is not a universally correct action. It is the action that works best once you fix what the opponent does, or what you believe about them, or what type they are, or what has already happened. The word given matters: given the opponent prices at ten dollars, I price at nine. Given the opponent plays heads half the time, I play tails half the time. Given I believe the opponent has high value, I bid higher. Every solution concept in game theory is built on this: set up a condition (the others' moves, beliefs, types, histories), compute the best response, and check that everyone is playing a best response to everyone else.
mathematical_intuition: Intuition for argmax: imagine all your options laid out. For each option, you write down the score you get if the opponent does what you expect. Then you pick the option with the highest score. That picked option (or options, if there is a tie) is your best response. The condition—what the opponent does—is not hidden. It is explicit in the score calculation.
student_trap: A trap is to discuss an action and forget what it is a best response to. You might say cutting price is good, but good against whom? If the rival cut first, cutting is best. If the rival did not cut, staying high might be better. The student has to train themselves to always ask: best response to what?
why_math_has_to_exist: Mathematics must exist because words alone cannot track the condition. When you say an action is best, the best-response set stores the answer in a clear form: these are the actions that score highest when the opponent does that specific thing. The set is reusable. You can take it, plug it into a Nash equilibrium check, or use it in an auction mechanism. It keeps the condition visible.
course_boundary_note: The boundary of best response is the condition. A best response is only correct after the opponent's action (or type, or belief about you, or history of play) has been specified. This is why every equilibrium concept in the course starts the same way: look locally at each player's best response to the others, then check globally that everyone is playing a best response to each other.

name: Nash Equilibrium
plain_language_definition: A situation where each person's chosen move is the best they can do given what everyone else is doing, so nobody has a reason to switch alone.
everyday_problem: You are trying to predict what a group of people will do when they are all trying to outthink each other. The problem is: your prediction only works if, after each person sees what you said the others would do, that person does not regret their own choice and decide to change.
first_principles_reason: A prediction about what rational people will do has to be self-consistent. If you predict a pattern and then one person, looking at that pattern, says "Wait, I could do better by switching," then your prediction breaks. Nash equilibrium is a prediction that survives this test.
mathematical_principle: The formal condition is: for every player i, their action a_i must be in the set BR_i(a_-i), meaning their action is among the best responses they could pick given what everyone else is doing. In other words, each player's move is the highest-scoring option available to them, given the others' moves.
why_it_matters: Nash equilibrium gives you a way to make a disciplined forecast about what will happen when each person is trying to do best for themselves. It does not say the outcome is fair or efficient—only that each person, acting alone, has no better move. This is the game-theory baseline for a prediction that holds up.
what_breaks_without_it: Without the Nash test, any outcome could be defended just by naming it. Someone could propose a pattern and offer no reason why each person would stick to it. Nash forces the question: if everyone else follows this pattern, does each individual want to follow it too?
naive_problem: A naive prediction looks at an outcome and says "This could happen" without asking the hard question: Once everyone else knows the pattern, does each participant still want to do their part? Nash adds that check.
failed_simple_approach: Simple approaches often focus on what is best for everyone combined, or what looks fair. But a pattern can be collectively good and still collapse if one person can sneak ahead by deviating alone. That is why we need the one-person test.
mathematical_object: The object is a profile—a list of each player's move—where every player's move is a best response to the others' moves. You can write it as a tuple or a list, but the key is that each component meets the best-response test.
operation: To check if a profile is Nash, go through each player one at a time. Hold everyone else's moves fixed and ask whether that player could improve by changing their move alone. If the answer is no for every player, you have a Nash equilibrium.
worked_mini_example: Two trucks arrive at a narrow bridge from opposite ends at the same time. If each truck driver thinks the other will wait, but each would rather go forward if the other waits, then neither will actually wait—both will try to cross and collide. A stable pattern is when each driver expects the other to do something specific and, based on that expectation, that driver's own choice makes sense. A stable pattern is one where each driver's move is their best response to what they expect.
lecture_emphasis: The course uses Nash equilibrium as the main tool for making predictions about rational strategic behavior. The real work is not memorizing the word; it is learning to check, player by player and scenario by scenario, whether each person would actually want to stick to a proposed pattern or switch.
common_misunderstanding: Many people hear equilibrium and think it means a good, fair, or efficient outcome. Nash equilibrium has no such promise. It can describe very bad outcomes—even prisoner's dilemma, where everyone loses—because it only cares about one thing: whether each person, acting alone, can do better. The outcome can be wasteful or unfair and still be Nash.
cross_course_connections: Nash equilibrium is where several earlier ideas come together. It uses best response (the idea that each player picks their highest-scoring move given the others). It connects forward to mixed strategies (where players sometimes roll dice to stay unpredictable), subgame perfection (equilibrium in every piece of a game tree), Bayesian Nash (equilibrium when players have private secrets), and perfect Bayesian equilibrium (combining both refinements). Each of these keeps the same core—no player wants to deviate alone—while handling a new complication like time, randomness, or hidden information.
recognize_in_new_work: In new situations, look for a pattern of behavior where no single participant can improve their own outcome by changing their own move alone, given that everyone else keeps doing what they are doing. When you spot that pattern, you have identified a candidate Nash equilibrium.
lecture_depth_walkthrough: To build understanding from the ground up: First, recognize that each player picks a move that scores best given what they expect others to do—that is best response. Now imagine a profile where best response closes the loop: everyone's action is a best response to everyone else's action. Each person reasons, "If they are all doing this, then my best choice is that." And that reasoning is true for every player at once. That is a Nash equilibrium. The course uses this idea to make a prediction that the course can stand behind. A proposed outcome is only a sound forecast if it survives each player asking in private, "Given what everyone else will do, do I want to stick to my part, or switch?" When you find a Nash equilibrium, you have found a prediction where every player, alone, has no reason to regret their move.
mathematical_intuition: Think of it as a mutual best-response loop. Each player's action sits inside their best-response set given everyone else's actions. Formally, a_i ∈ BR_i(a_-i) for all i. Intuitively, imagine you hold everyone's moves still and ask each player in turn, "Would you change?" If nobody would change, the profile is Nash. The condition is symmetric across players: nobody has an escape route.
student_trap: A common trap is to confuse Nash equilibrium with a good outcome or a balanced state. Students hear equilibrium and imagine something stable and fair. But a Nash equilibrium can be the worst outcome available, unfair, or wasteful. It only guarantees one narrow thing: no single player can unilaterally improve. Do not expect it to be nice.
why_math_has_to_exist: Strategic prediction is circular. Each player's best move depends on what others do, which depends on what each of them expects, which depends on what everyone expects the first player to do. The model needs a fixed point where all these expectations and moves fit together. Nash equilibrium is that fixed point—it is the formal answer to the question, "What profile survives the logical loop of mutual best response?"
course_boundary_note: Nash equilibrium checks one thing: unilateral deviation. It does not handle threats that are not credible, does not account for players learning and changing beliefs over time, does not allow groups of players to conspire together, and does not evaluate whether the outcome is fair without additional work. Know what it does and does not do.

name: Mixed Strategies
plain_language_definition: You deliberately flip a coin or roll dice to decide your move, so the other player cannot predict what you will do and use that prediction against you.
everyday_problem: You face a jam: if you always pick one move, the other player learns this and beats you every time. But there might not be any single move you can stick to that is safe. So you need a way to stay unpredictable while still being smart about it.
first_principles_reason: Randomness itself becomes a weapon. If you pick randomly from a few moves in exactly the right proportions, you can make your opponent face a choice where neither of their moves is better than the other. They cannot exploit you because there is no pattern to find.
mathematical_principle: When you do not know what the other player will do, you assign a probability—a chance—to each possibility. Then you add up your score across all those possibilities, weighted by how likely each is. In symbols: your expected payoff = (probability of outcome A) times (score from A) plus (probability of outcome B) times (score from B), and so on. This way you can compare your options by their average payoff, not just their best or worst case.
why_it_matters: If you are predictable, people punish you. When no pure action—no single move you always pick—can be stable, deliberate mixing is the answer. You randomize in the exact right way so that your opponent has no profitable switch, because you have made all their options equally good.
what_breaks_without_it: The course would wrongly claim some games have no stable answer just because players cannot both pick fixed pure moves and stand still. It would also miss that randomness can be a choice, not just noise or confusion.
naive_problem: A naive person thinks mixing means you are confused or do not have a plan. The course points out that you can have a deliberate, calculated probability distribution for your moves that your opponent cannot crack.
failed_simple_approach: The simple approach—just pick one move and stick with it—fails in games like pennies, where whatever you pick, your opponent has a profitable response. To survive against a smart opponent, you must make every move they could respond to look equally bad from their angle, and that forces you to mix.
mathematical_object: The mathematical object is a probability distribution: a list of your pure moves, each with a number between 0 and 1 (the chance you pick it), and they add up to 1. Often, the equilibrium distribution makes your opponent indifferent—unable to gain by switching between the moves they use.
operation: Write down how happy your opponent would be if you picked each of your moves some probability. Calculate their expected payoff if they respond with each of their moves. Pick probabilities for your moves that make your opponent's expected payoffs equal for the responses they would actually use, so they have no reason to lean harder on one.
worked_mini_example: In a penalty kick, if the shooter always shoots left, the goalie dives left and saves it. If the shooter mixes—sometimes left, sometimes right—in the right ratio (say 50-50), then diving left saves as many as diving right does, on average. The goalie cannot gain by picking a side, so both the shooter's left-shot and right-shot remain part of the equilibrium.
lecture_emphasis: The lecture teaches you to solve for the exact probabilities that make the other player willing to mix. Indifference—the other player being unable to pick a better response—is not a side detail. It is the key equation that locks in the mixture.
common_misunderstanding: Many people think mixing means you do not know what you are doing. In the model, you deliberately choose the distribution and commit to it. The randomness is calculated and intentional, not accidental.
cross_course_connections: Mixed strategies tie together Nash equilibrium (a stable resting point where no single player wants to move), zero-sum games (one player's gain is the other's loss), minimax (the worst average result you can guarantee yourself), and expected utility (what you expect to win on average). When you mix, you are not picking one payoff; you are choosing a distribution whose average results shape what the opponent can do.
recognize_in_new_work: Look for indifference equations—places where the other player has no reason to prefer one response to another. Look for randomized play or models where any predictable behavior would be punished by someone who sees it.
lecture_depth_walkthrough: The deep lecture asks why someone would randomize on purpose. The answer: in some games, any pure move—any single action—can be exploited. A mixed strategy turns your decision into a probability distribution over actions. The equilibrium mixture often makes your opponent indifferent among the moves they are willing to use. Randomness is therefore a choice, not noise. It changes your opponent's payoff arithmetic, which changes what can stay stable.
mathematical_intuition: The intuition comes from expected payoff under probabilities. If your opponent mixes, then each pure action you might pick has an expected payoff. In equilibrium, actions that you use with positive probability must usually earn the same expected payoff. If one action were better, you would shift your probability weight toward it, which would make your opponent want to shift too, breaking equilibrium.
student_trap: Students ask: what does the player actually choose? The answer: the player chooses the distribution itself. Once the random device rolls—once an action happens—the distribution was already the commitment. The mix is the strategy, not a mistake.
why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object must exist because pure actions do not always allow stable predictions. A probability distribution over actions lets you control your own predictability. The distribution becomes your strategy because it decides your opponent's expected payoffs before the random roll happens.
course_boundary_note: The boundary is about what a mixed strategy really means and when it applies.
